newsitem.title: USA: Titanium sector unfazed by Boeing-McDonnell merger.
newsitem.headline: Titanium sector unfazed by Boeing-McDonnell merger.

text.p: The big three U.S. titanium producers, whose fortunes largely depend on aerospace, gave a collective thumbs up to the multi-billion dollar merger of Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas.
Producers of the light metal brushed aside fears that a huge consumer of their output may use stronger buying clout to keep prices competitive.
"I think for the American aerospace industry it's a good move," said David Floyd, commercial manager at Oregon Metallurgical Corp. "It appeared that McDonnell Douglas was in trouble."
Joe Compofelice, chief financial officer at Titanium Metals, saw a good match between McDonnell Douglas' spare capacity and Boeing's heavy order book.
"If this helps the combined entity deliver planes to the airlines faster, then this is a net positive for the entire titanium industry," Compofelice said.
John Odle, executive vice president of RMI Titanium Co, welcomed the tie up and said Boeing and McDonnell already had so much buying clout before the merger.
"You reach a point where how much more clout can you have," Odle said. "I think in some cases the merger may be helpful, especially if they consolidate specifications and dimensions for products."

All three U.S. producers expected no real change in the relationship between the titanium industry and its customers, whether they dealt directly with Boeing or indirectly through forgings and components makers.
Analysts said the merger did not appear to be a huge positive for the titanium sector, but neither was there any major negative overspill.
"On paper, in theory, there is more muscle in terms of buying clout, but backlogs already go out quite a way," Lehman Brother's titanium stocks analyst Richard Aldrich said.
"I don't sense any quaking on the part of the titanium guys," Aldrich said. "The industry was pretty concentrated as it was."
McDonnell Douglas and Boeing agreed last month to work together on developing a new generation of wide-bodied jets which would need more titanium in their construction than the present range.
The post-merger fate of this deal was unclear.

"The golf industry is really Boeing's biggest competitor these days, I guess," Aldrich said, referring to the heady growth in titanium golf driver heads, siphoning metal at a time of huge aircraft orders.
Commercial aircraft consume about 36 percent of the 100 million pounds or so of titanium products made annually.
The turnaround in the commercial aircraft sector fueled the titanium stock's recent takeoff into the black.
